newsitem.title: JAPAN: FORECAST-Japan Jan c/a expected to show deficit.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Japan Jan c/a expected to show deficit.

text.p: Japan's current account is expected to show a deficit of about 31 billion yen in January, the first deficit in six years, compared with a surplus of 32.6 billion yen a year earlier, economists said on Monday.
A Reuters poll gave forecasts ranging from a deficit of 96.2 billion yen to a surplus of 40 billion yen. The current account is the broadest measure of trade in goods and services.
The January current account figures are due to be released at 8.50 a.m. on Thursday (2350 GMT Wednesday).

Economists said the data would be exaggerated by seasonal factors. January trade figures are unpredictable as the length of the New Year holidays, including weekends, varies from year to year, affecting the number of business days.

The overall trade surplus, a major component of the current account, is expected to have fallen sharply in January as Japanese firms refrained from exports in the first few days of the month due to the New Year's holidays.

The current account surplus on an unadjusted basis has been steadily falling over the last two years as the yen's appreciation against the dollar until the middle of 1995 curbed exports while helping to boost imports.

But a weaker yen against the dollar since then has helped to push up Japan's exports, slowing down the pace of the year-on-year decline in Japan's overall current account surplus. Japan's trade surplus with the United States has also risen sharply in recent months, leading U.S. officials to express concern.

Last Friday, Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers warned Japan against trying to export its way out of its economic problems and urged it to restore domestic demand-led growth and repair its financial system.
Peter Morgan, an economist at HSBC James Capel Japan, said the current account surplus may have bottomed out in April last year on a seasonally adjusted basis.
"The surplus (on an unadjusted basis) will be rising by the second quarter this year... If we see the surplus rising sharply, that could lead to trade friction," Morgan said.
Forecasts by individual research firms are as follows:
Daiwa Bank Research 96.2 billion yen deficit
HSBC James Capel Japan 75 billion yen deficit
BZW 50 billion yen deficit
Lehman Brothers 39.6 billion yen deficit
Nippon Credit Bank 30 billion yen deficit
Merrill Lynch Japan 20 billion yen deficit
Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan 16.2 billion yen deficit
Yamaichi Research Institute 5 billion yen surplus
Salomon Brothers Asia 40 billion yen surplus
